4.1 — The Enemy: Patrol

The turret never moves. The enemy hunts — and a hunt starts with something calmer: a guard walking a beat, back and forth, forever, with no marker in the scene to walk it against. Today you decide what "back and forth" actually means, give the enemy the body it does not have, and build the calmest half of the machine you will finish in 4.5.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make an enemy follow a patrol route?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

The enemy should walk a beat — back and forth, forever, with nobody at the keyboard. "Make the enemy patrol" is the whole feature, and at this moment the enemy is a picture with an empty script on it: no wall can stop it, and it has never moved once.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the enemy a bodyA Collider2D on the prefab root, sized by hand against art that lives on a child, plus a Rigidbody2D with Body Type Dynamic and Gravity Scale 0 — the same pair you gave the Player in 2.1. Until both exist, no wall can stop the enemy and no collision message will ever fire on it, which is exactly what 4.4 needs.Read: the Collider2D and Rigidbody2D rows and the Body Type warning in the quick reference, and the recipe you followed for the Player in 2.1.
  2. write this partRead: the [SerializeField] private Transform row of the API table below, and the field that remembered a moment on the turret in 3.3.
  3. Move it toward the end it is holdingEvery frame: subtract the two positions to get an arrow, normalize it so the enemy does not sprint when it is far away, multiply by a speed and hand the result to the body. Velocity is measured per second, so that line takes no Time.deltaTime.Read: the (a - b).normalized row and the rb.linearVelocity = v row in the quick reference — the pair you used on the diagonal in 1.5 and on the Player in 2.2.
  4. Notice it has arrived, and turn aroundThe distance check from 3.1, against a small threshold instead of a radius. When it is true, the field from part 2 is handed the other end of the beat — nothing about the enemy moves at that moment, only that field changes.Read: the Vector3.Distance row in the quick reference, and the range check you wrote on the turret in 3.1.

Three of those four parts are work you have already done: a collider and a Dynamic body is 2.1, a normalized direction and a velocity is 2.2, and a distance compared against a threshold is 3.1. Only one part has no precedent at all, and it is the smallest one: until today everything this game remembered was a number that changed — a coin count, health, a moment on the clock. Today the memory is where you are going, and the turn is nothing more than that memory changing. That is the whole reason a beat can run with nobody at the keyboard: a player turns because a key was pressed, and the enemy has no keys.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make an enemy patrol" cannot be looked up. "Move an object toward a position at a constant speed" can — and you wrote that line in 2.2.

Your turn

The reading prices three ways to define a beat. Which did you choose, and what does your choice cost you — in your own words, not the table's?

A patrolling enemy has no keyboard. Name one thing the Player gets from Input that the enemy now has to keep in a field instead.

The Problem: A Guard With No Memory ~20 min

Select Assets/Prefabs/MobileEnemy and read its Inspector. Notice what it has — a Transform, an empty EnemyController component, and a child object — and then notice what it does not have. Compare it against the Player, which has carried a collider and a body since 2.1. Write down the difference before you read on.

Now the design question. An enemy that walks back and forth forever must remember something. A player who is not pressing keys simply stops; an enemy left alone has to keep going and know when to turn. So: what is the smallest amount of state that produces a beat? Work it out before you look at the options — the answer is smaller than you think.

Here are the three honest ways to define where a beat begins and ends:

How the beat is definedWhat the enemy storesHow the turn happensWhat it costs
A leash from where it spawned Two facts and nothing else: the position it started at, and how far it is allowed to wander. Measure how far it has drifted from that anchor — Vector3.Distance(transform.position, anchorPosition), the same call you used on the turret in 3.1 — and when the distance exceeds the leash, flip the stored sign: direction = -direction; No scene setup whatsoever, and the beat follows the enemy wherever you drag it. But the beat is always centred on the spawn point and is always a straight line — it cannot follow a corridor around a corner. The turn is also only noticed after the enemy has moved, so it always overshoots the limit by up to one frame of travel.
Two placed waypoints Two Transforms — usually two empty objects, wired into two Inspector slots. Walk toward the current waypoint; when you are close enough, swap which one is the target: if (Vector3.Distance(transform.position, target.position) < 0.1f) { target = other; } You must create, place and wire the objects, and invent an "arrived" threshold that is small enough to be accurate but not so small the enemy jitters — if one frame of travel is longer than that threshold, the enemy walks straight past the waypoint and never turns at all. In exchange, the beat can be any shape: corners, long routes, a loop of three or more points.
Absolute bounds Two numbers: a minimum and a maximum. If the position passes either bound, reverse — if (transform.position.y > topLimit) { direction = -1; } The simplest maths of the three, and the most brittle. Those bounds are world coordinates: move the enemy in the scene and its beat stays behind. Drop a copy of the prefab somewhere else and it will turn on the very first frame. The new value also has to be one the sign is allowed to hold: the moment a bug lets it become 0, the enemy stops walking and the beat is over.
The round IS the behaviour. Nobody is watching a guard on a beat, and that is exactly why the walk has to be worth watching on its own: a beat that reads as a twitch looks like a bug, and a beat the player can predict reads as a guard. No line of code decides which of those you get — the speed, the length of the beat and any pause at each end do. The animation you build in 4.2 is only ever animating the beat you write today.

Whichever you choose, the enemy is still a picture. Before it can be stopped by a wall — or touch the player at all in 4.4 — you have to give it a body. Here is what your options cost:

Body setup for the enemyWhat the player experiencesWhat it requires of your code
No collider, no Rigidbody2D — what it ships with The enemy walks through walls, through the player, through everything. It is a ghost. Nothing. And that is the problem: no collision messages will ever fire on it, so the contact damage in 4.4 becomes impossible to build.
Collider + Dynamic Rigidbody2D, Gravity Scale 0 The enemy is solid and is stopped by walls — but only if your movement respects physics. You must use a movement method from the 2.2 table that consults the physics engine. Gravity Scale must be zero, exactly as you set it on the top-down player.
Collider + Kinematic Rigidbody2D Completely stable — no gravity, no tumbling, no drift — but the walls of your scene are not solid to it. A Kinematic body only collides with Dynamic bodies, so it patrols straight through every static collider on the map and nothing can push it. Kinematic bodies ignore forces and velocity, so you must move it with MovePosition or by transform — and MovePosition will not stop it at a wall either. With no wall able to turn it, the whole beat has to be enforced in your code.
The enemy's visible sprite is on a child object. The MobileEnemy root carries no Sprite Renderer — the art lives on a child called Sprite, offset slightly and scaled up. A default collider added to the root is sized from nothing and will not cover the enemy you can see. This is the same trap as the Coin in 2.1, and it is worth pressing Play and watching a bullet sail through the visible body once, so you never make the mistake twice.

Socratic: Designing a Beat

  1. Which of the three beat definitions fits an enemy you will place four or five times across a map and keep nudging while you design the level? What does your choice cost you?
  2. The leash approach stores the position the enemy started at. Which lifecycle method must save it, and what would the enemy do if you saved it every frame instead?
  3. A single int holding 1 or -1 is the enemy's entire memory of where it is going. Why is that enough — and what extra state would a bool such as isGoingRight force you to keep in sync?
Read the Docs: The API for a Beat ~15 min

Every row below is a call or a declaration you have already typed somewhere in this course. Read the last column as carefully as the middle one: the rows with no surprises in them are the rows whose costs you have already met once, and the costs are the whole reason this lesson is a decision rather than a recipe.

APIWhat it gives youWhat it costs
[SerializeField] private Transform waypoint; A slot in the Inspector holding a reference to another object. An empty GameObject's Transform is a place in the scene, so one slot can hold one end of a beat. The same declaration form you have used since 1.3. An empty slot does not complain when you press Play — it throws at the moment your code reads it, which looks like a patrol bug and is really a wiring bug. And a slot belongs to the object it sits on: wired on the prefab, all four enemies share one beat; wired on an instance, that one differs.
Vector3.Distance(a, b) The straight-line distance between two points — the call that decided whether the turret could see you in 3.1, and now the call that decides whether the enemy has arrived. It measures between two positions, so both have to exist. Ask it about a null waypoint and the script stops with a NullReferenceException — one every frame, in the Console, pointing at that line.
(a - b).normalized Subtracting two positions gives the arrow from one to the other; normalizing throws its length away and leaves pure direction. The diagonal fix from 1.5, reused to aim a projectile in 3.2. Miss it out and the arrow is as long as the distance, so "direction × speed" quietly becomes a speed that grows with the gap. The enemy sprints when it is far from the waypoint and never arrives cleanly — and nothing about the line looks wrong.
Rigidbody2D.linearVelocity = v Hand the movement to the physics engine — your movement method from 2.2, and the only reason a wall can stop the enemy at all. It is measured in units per second, so it takes no Time.deltaTime; add one and the enemy's speed starts depending on your frame rate. Unity 6 renamed this from velocity, so tutorials written before then will not compile.
transform.position Where the enemy is right now — one half of every distance you measure, and the thing the waypoints are compared against. Reading it is free. Writing to it is the trap: it moves the object without telling the physics engine, which is exactly how the Player walked through the level in 1.4. When a body owns the movement, nothing else may write the position.
All three approaches are the same four parts in different clothes. A body a wall can stop, one field that remembers which way the enemy is walking, one movement line that consults the physics engine, and one distance check that changes that field. The leash calls the field a sign; the waypoints call it a target; the bounds call it a limit. The walkthrough below builds the waypoint version, and if you chose a different row you are still building those four parts — the differences between the rows are exactly what the table above priced.

Predict Before Building

  1. The leash row measures a distance that grows and shrinks forever. If you flip the sign the moment the drift exceeds the leash, the enemy is already past the limit when it turns. How far past — and what decides that?
  2. The waypoint row compares a distance against a small threshold. What goes wrong if you set that threshold to zero, and what goes wrong if you set it to five on a two-metre route?
  3. The bounds row reverses using a stored sign. What are the only two values that sign may hold, and what happens if a bug lets it become zero?
Build It With MeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I make an enemy follow a patrol route?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs. The enemy ships as a stub: an empty EnemyController on a prefab with no collider and no body, standing in the Overworld four times over. Today it gets a body, two waypoints and one field that remembers which end of the beat it is walking toward. The movement line is the one you chose in 2.2 — if you move your Player a different way, keep your method and read the shape.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Give it a body — this step is not code

No collider and no body means no wall will ever stop the enemy and no collision message will ever fire on it. That is also why this comes first: nothing you write in the rest of this lesson can work without it.

// Assets/Prefabs/MobileEnemy ▸ the Inspector

Collider 2D        (added to the ROOT, sized by hand)
Rigidbody 2D ▸ Body Type   =  Dynamic
Rigidbody 2D ▸ Gravity Scale =  0
Rigidbody 2D ▸ Freeze Rotation Z = ON
  1. 1Everything in this step happens on the prefab, not in the script. Select it in the Project window and read the Inspector: a Transform, an empty EnemyController, and one child object.
  2. 3Add the collider to the root — the object the EnemyController script sits on. Then drag its handles in the Scene view until the green outline covers the enemy you can actually see, and press Play with no patrol code at all to watch what happens when you walk into it.The art is not on the root. The MobileEnemy root has no Sprite Renderer at all; the picture lives on a child called *Sprite*, offset slightly and scaled up. A collider added to the root is sized from nothing, so its outline is a small square in the middle of a much bigger body — and in 4.4 the player will be able to stand inside the visible enemy and take no damage. Same trap as the Coin in 2.1.
  3. 4The component that puts the enemy into the physics simulation, with the one body type the world can stop.Only a Dynamic body is stopped by the world — the rule you met in 2.1 and had to repair in 2.2. Kinematic is the body type the Unity docs recommend for scripted movement, and it is the one body type that passes through every static collider on the map in complete silence.
  4. 5The same value you set on the Player in 2.1, for the same reason: the Overworld is seen from above and has no *down*.The default is 1. Leave it and the moment you press Play the enemy falls off the bottom of the scene — and because it stops patrolling while it falls, it looks like a script bug rather than a setting.
  5. 6The setting you turned on for the Player in 2.2, for the same reason a Dynamic body needs it.Without it, one shove from the player leaves the enemy spinning for the rest of the run — and the sprite spins with it, because the art is on the child.

Step 2Declare the two ends of the beat and the numbers that tune it

Four lines in the class body, and every one of them is a line a designer can see in the Inspector — the [SerializeField] pattern from 1.3.

    [SerializeField] private Transform waypointA;
    [SerializeField] private Transform waypointB;
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 2f;
    [SerializeField] private float arriveDistance = 0.1f;

    private Rigidbody2D body;
  1. 1One end of the beat. A Transform holds a position in the world — and, wired from the Inspector, it holds a *reference to another object*, which is what a waypoint slot is. Two empty GameObjects placed in the scene are enough.Slots, not typed-in coordinates. A waypoint is a place in the scene, so it belongs to the scene: you can drag either end while the game is running and watch the beat move. Two hard-coded x values would give you the same straight line and break the moment you moved the prefab somewhere else.
  2. 2The other end. Two slots rather than one, because a beat has two ends and the enemy has to be able to reach both.
  3. 3How fast it walks, in units per second — the same kind of knob, with the same name, as moveSpeed on your Player. A reader of your project should not have to learn a second word for the same idea.
  4. 4How close counts as arrived — the number that decides when the beat turns around.It has to be small enough that the enemy looks like it reached the waypoint, and large enough that it can actually *reach* it. An enemy that travels further in one frame than this number walks straight past the waypoint and never arrives at all — and when the beat is wrong, this is one of the two numbers you will be tuning.
  5. 6A place to keep the reference to the enemy's own body, so the movement line in step 4 does not have to search for it every frame. You keep one of these on the Player for exactly the same reason — 2.2 says look it up once.

Step 3Declare the memory, and give it a value before the first frame

Start() runs once, before Update() has ever run — you already use it in 2.2 for the Player's body lookup, and the enemy's stub already has the method waiting.

    private Transform target;
    void Start()
    {
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();
        target = waypointB;
    }
  1. 1The memory. One field holding which end of the beat the enemy is walking toward right now. It is the only thing in the file that changes when the enemy turns around.Notice that it has no value yet — the next lines give it one. And notice where it lives: in the class body, not inside Update(). Move this line into a method and it is rebuilt from nothing sixty times a second, so the enemy can never remember which way it was going. That is the scope rule from 1.3, and it is the same mistake that would break lastAttackTime in 3.3.
  2. 2The once-only setup method from 1.3. EnemyController ships as an empty stub, so this method is yours to fill.
  3. 4Finds the Rigidbody2D you added in step 1 and keeps the reference. GetComponent is the lookup from 2.1, and calling it once in Start() instead of every frame is the rule from 2.2.Without this line the movement in step 4 has nothing to write to. The field would still be empty, and the Console fills with a NullReferenceException on the first frame, pointing at the line that uses the body. An empty reference is a valid value in C# — nothing complains until you use it.
  4. 5Seeds the memory, so the enemy knows which way it is walking before the first frame runs. Either end works; starting toward B gives a full first beat.Leave this out and the first frame throws. A field with no value is null, and the arrival check in step 4 asks that reference for its position. Same argument as seeding the turret's timer in 3.3: the memory needs a value before anything reads it — and the value has to come from somewhere that runs *once*.
  5. 6Closes Start().

Step 4Walk toward it every frame, and turn when you get there

Two jobs, and together they are the whole beat: go toward the end you are holding, and — when you have arrived — hold the other one.

    void Update()
    {
        Vector2 direction = (target.position - transform.position).normalized;
        body.linearVelocity = direction * moveSpeed;

        if (Vector3.Distance(transform.position, target.position) < arriveDistance)
        {
________________
        }
    }
  1. 1The every-frame method, and the reason a beat can run with nobody at the keyboard. Update() is what keeps going when no input arrives.
  2. 3The arrow from the enemy to the waypoint it is walking toward, at a length of exactly 1: subtract the two positions, then normalize — the pair you used on the diagonal in 1.5 and to aim a projectile in 3.2.Do not skip .normalized. Without it the vector is as long as the distance to the waypoint, so the enemy sprints when it is far away and creeps when it is close — and on a long beat it covers the whole waypoint in a single frame and never arrives. A position is a Vector3 and a velocity is a Vector2; Unity converts between them by dropping z, which is harmless in a flat world.
  3. 4Hands the body a velocity instead of moving the Transform yourself — the movement method you chose from the 2.2 table, and the only reason a wall can stop the enemy at all.No Time.deltaTime on this line. Velocity is measured in units *per second*, so the physics engine already applies the time for you. Multiply by deltaTime and the enemy's speed starts depending on your frame rate — the identical mistake 2.2 killed on the Player.
  4. 6The arrival test: the distance check from 3.1, with the threshold you declared in step 2 instead of a radius. True on every frame the enemy is standing within arriveDistance of the waypoint it was walking toward.
  5. Your turn8The turn. The enemy has arrived at the waypoint it was walking toward — hand the memory from step 3 the OTHER end of the beat. Nothing else about the enemy changes at this moment: not its position, not its speed, not the waypoints. An if/else you already know is enough to write it.The field holds which end it is walking toward. Ask it which one it is holding right now — a Transform can be compared with == — and send it to the other. Both waypoints are in scope, and only one of them is the right answer on any given frame.Leave this line out and the enemy walks to the first waypoint and stands there forever. Nothing else in the file ends the journey: on the Player, letting go of the keys was the turn, and the enemy has no keys. And a line that always writes the same waypoint is only one beat — it arrives, sends itself back to the place it is already standing, and never walks again. The two ends have to alternate, which means the line has to *ask* what the field is holding.
  6. 10Closes Update(). One more } closes the class.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. The gap is the turn, and it is the one line in this lesson with nothing earlier to copy: the field remembers which end of the beat the enemy is heading for, and the turn is that field changing its mind. This file writes it as a small method with an if/else, and turns *before* it walks where the walkthrough turns after — on every frame but the one where the enemy arrives, those two orders are the same file, and any form that hands the field the *other* waypoint is correct. Your waypoint placement, your speed, your threshold and your movement method from 2.2 are yours; the shape is what has to match.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

// EnemyController.cs — one guard, one beat, forever.
// The two ends of the beat are objects in the scene. This script keeps exactly
// one thing about the walk: which end it is heading for. The turn is that
// field changing its mind.
public class EnemyController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private Transform waypointA;           // one end of the beat
    [SerializeField] private Transform waypointB;           // the other end
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 2f;          // units per SECOND
    [SerializeField] private float arriveDistance = 0.1f;   // how close is "there"

    private Transform target;                               // which way it is walking
    private Rigidbody2D body;

    void Start()
    {
        // Looked up once, never inside Update() — the rule from 2.2.
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();

        // Seed the memory. Either end works; this one gives a full first beat.
        target = waypointB;
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // Arrive first, walk second. The order only matters on the one frame
        // where the enemy reaches a waypoint.
        if (Vector3.Distance(transform.position, target.position) < arriveDistance)
        {
            TurnAround();
        }

        // No Time.deltaTime: velocity is per second, not per frame (2.2).
        Vector2 direction = (target.position - transform.position).normalized;
        body.linearVelocity = direction * moveSpeed;
    }

    // The only thing that ends a beat. The player lets go of the keys; the
    // enemy has no keys, so the turn has to be written here.
    private void TurnAround()
    {
        if (target == waypointA)
        {
            target = waypointB;
        }
        else
        {
            target = waypointA;
        }
    }
}

// Inspector, on Assets/Prefabs/MobileEnemy:
//   Collider 2D                       =  on the ROOT, resized by hand until the
//                                        outline covers the art on the Sprite child
//   Rigidbody 2D ▸ Body Type          =  Dynamic   <- only Dynamic is stopped by walls
//   Rigidbody 2D ▸ Gravity Scale      =  0         <- the Overworld has no down
//   Rigidbody 2D ▸ Freeze Rotation Z  =  ON        <- solid hits impart spin
//   Waypoint A / Waypoint B           =  two empty GameObjects placed in the scene
Build Lab: Give It a Beat ~30 min

Step 1 — find your enemies. The Overworld scene already contains four MobileEnemy instances. Count them yourself in the Hierarchy before you add anything, and note where each one sits. There is exactly one Coin in that scene. You may move the enemies, and you may drag more from Assets/Prefabs if your design needs them — but count first, so you know what you actually changed.

Step 2 — give it a body. Add the collider and the body you chose to the MobileEnemy prefab, and set Gravity Scale deliberately. Then press Play with no patrol code at all and walk into it. Find out whether it is solid yet.

Step 3 — build your beat. The walkthrough above built the waypoint pair, step by step. If that is the row you chose, your remaining work is the waypoints themselves: create the two objects, wire the slots, and tune the speed and the threshold against the size of the Overworld. If you chose the leash or the bounds, this is where you build yours — the five decisions below are the same five for every row, and the answers look nothing alike.

Architectural specification for EnemyController.cs:

The body — whichever beat you chose:

  • Which two components does the prefab need before a wall can stop the enemy, and which of the two does the script need before it can hear anything from the physics engine? Which object do they go on?
  • The visible enemy is not on the root. How will you size the collider against the art you can see, and how do you check that in the Scene view rather than by guessing?
  • What Body Type and what Gravity Scale did you set, and which of the two decides whether a wall stops the enemy at all?

The ends of the beat:

  • What does your row store — a spawn anchor plus a distance, two waypoint Transforms, or two numbers? What does each of those cost you when you duplicate the enemy across the map?
  • If you chose the leash, what does the anchor mean to a designer moving the enemy around the scene? Say it in one sentence a level designer would understand.
  • If you chose waypoints, where do the two empty objects live — children of the enemy, or separate objects in the scene? What breaks about each choice when you duplicate the enemy?

The memory — one field, and the whole beat hangs off it:

  • What single field records which way the enemy is walking? What type is smallest for your row, and what value does it start at?
  • If your row stores a sign, which arithmetic operation reverses it, and why is that cheaper than an if that assigns the opposite value? What are the only two values it may ever hold?
  • If your row stores a waypoint, how does the turn choose the other one — and what is left of the beat if that line keeps writing the same one?
  • Whichever your row: where does that field live, inside Update() or in the class body? Say what breaks if you get it wrong, using the word "frame" in your answer.

The movement:

  • Which movement call do you use — the one you chose for the player in 2.2, or a different one? Whatever you pick, how do you keep the speed frame-rate independent?
  • A top-down enemy could patrol on either axis. Which axis does your design use, and what single character in your movement line decides that?
  • What has to be true of the enemy's body before your movement line has anything to write to, and where is that lookup done — once, or every frame?

The turn:

  • Which measurement decides that the beat has ended, and which of the three rows does it belong to?
  • Which comparison operator do you use at the boundary — and what would the enemy do at exactly the boundary with the other one?
  • What number decides "close enough"? What happens if it is smaller than the distance the enemy travels in a single frame?
  • How do you report each turn to the Console so you can watch the beat without a UI?

Save and press Play. Watch one full beat end to end. The enemy should walk one way, turn, walk back, and repeat — forever, with no input from you.

  • Explain the one field that is your enemy's whole memory of where it is going, and the single line that changes its mind
  • Explain why the enemy's collider cannot go on the root object as-is
